newsitem.title: GERMANY: Opposition leader Lafontaine gains stature in Bonn.
newsitem.headline: Opposition leader Lafontaine gains stature in Bonn.

text.p: It seems to have taken cooperation talks with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government to give opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leader Oskar Lafontaine the aura of a man who could take power in Bonn.

After years of developing a reputation as a radical thinker and unpredictable politician, Lafontaine has for now succeeded where several SPD leaders before him failed, silencing internal quarrels and focusing attacks on a fragile government.
Even his arch-rival, ambitious Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, said in a recent interview that Lafontaine was the SPD's strongest leader since the legendary Willy Brandt.

"There's little dissent in the party right now. More than that, Lafontaine is for the first time visibly showing himself in the tax talks as a serious, reliable figure," said Professor Hans-Joachim Veen of the conservative Konrad Adenauer Foundation.

The SPD agreed to talks with Kohl's government on a planned tax reform when a leap of half a million in the unemployment total forced it to show that it was ready to take some responsibility and not just block government plans.

But where other SPD leaders would have faced a chorus of divergent demands, Lafontaine has earned plaudits within the party for orchestrating a rare show of unity that has at last let the SPD capitalise on government weakness.

After trailing badly in most opinion polls for over two years, surveys now indicate that if an election were held immediately, a centre-left coalition of SPD and environmentalist Greens would oust Kohl's centre-right alliance.

Analysts and party officials detect a new maturity in Lafontaine, who lost dismally to Kohl as the SPD's candidate in the 1990 election. His insistence on the high cost of unification and the need for ecological reform completely missed the euphoric mood of the nation.
He then did himself no favours in the SPD by turning down the party leadership.
But since he finally became chairman in a spectacular leadership coup 14 months ago, Lafontaine has shown a new readiness to work more subtly behind the scenes.

Unlike predecessor Rudolf Scharping, Lafontaine has not yielded to the temptation to declare he wants to stand against Kohl in 1998, or commit himself to a coalition with the environmentalist Greens if the SPD should win.
"I'm sure he's had to work hard to discipline himself as well as the party," said Professor Dietrich Thraenhardt of Muenster University.
By not giving his opponents a target to aim at, he has effectively laid the groundwork for both these aims, and is shaking off his 1990 "loser" image.

Lafontaine's own aides and most analysts say he has succeeded in subtly undermining any challenge from Schroeder, should he decide early next year to contest Lafontaine's right to be the SPD's chancellery candidate in October 1998.
While Schroeder regularly tops polls as the man most likely to beat Kohl in a direct contest, Lafontaine is catching up.

At the same time, he has extracted hints from the government that it might be interested, as part of its own tax reform, in implementing some of Lafontaine's trademark policies, such as raising tax on energy consumption and trying to boost consumer spending.
That in turn could lay the groundwork for the coalition with the Greens which Lafontaine still dreams of, but is reluctant to advertise for fear of giving his opponents an easy target.
"There's no doubt Lafontaine wants to govern with the Greens, and with the polls looking the way they do, you wouldn't rule it out," Veen said.
